articles.title: Chicago is getting a self-cleaning public restroom. Where is it, and when can it be used?
articles.description: The West Town neighborhood now has the city's first public toilet. It's just not open for use yet. Ald. Daniel La Spata's (1st) office did not have an estimated completion date for when the toilet will be installed since the project was announced last October . But it has raised questions about how it will work, be managed, and who will pay for it. Here's what you need to know. Where can I find the toilet? Chicago's sole public bathroom popped up this week near the CTA Blue Line station in the Polish Triangle at Division Street and Ashland and Milwaukee Avenues in West Town. Foundation work at the site is complete and contractors are working to attach utilities before restoration of the immediate area begins, according to La Spata’s office. How does it work? The public toilets like the one in West Town are free to use, but have a time limit and are automatically cleaned between uses. A combination of water and disinfectant is sprayed across the floor to clean anything left behind. Two toilet bowls are then rotated out to be disinfected by a power wash system. Newer models can clean in 30 seconds, according to the French company JCDecaux, though older models took up to five minutes to disinfect between uses. Who produces the toilet? Who is paying for it? JCDecaux, a French outdoor advertising company, is providing the restroom and maintenance at no cost to the city through a pilot program. However, the more than $400,000 in plumbing and installation costs will be covered with the 1st Ward’s menu funds — which City Council members receive annually for infrastructure projects in their ward — according to La Spata's office. The company currently holds a three-year, $700,000 contract with the CTA through October 2027 to install and maintain screens displaying arrival times at city bus stations, which is an extension of previous contracts dating as far back as 2002, according to city records. In addition to Chicago, JCDecaux has previously supplied 25 standalone public toilets to San Francisco since 1994, and New York has seven already installed with plans to bring that number to 40 total. Last year, the company replaced 417 of the 435 self-cleaning restrooms it had installed in Paris with newer models. It also maintains 278 of the restrooms in Berlin that are among the 2,500 toilets it manages globally. In San Francisco, the company signed a 20-year agreement to take on the full cost of design, manufacturing, installation and daily maintenance of toilets in exchange for installing 114 advertising screens and kiosks around the city. One of JCDecaux’s self-cleaning public restrooms in Paris, France. JCDecaux Why is there a public toilet need? Chicago, like many other cities, has struggled with bathroom access. A 2021 report by the Chicago Tribune identified fewer than 500 structures in the city with free public restrooms, with most located in libraries, police stations, parks and other public buildings. Officials globally have noted that the lack of public restrooms is particularly a problem for parents of young children, pregnant people, seniors, people with medical conditions and unhoused people. JCDecaux has supported the idea that access to hygiene is a human right. New York is among several cities to have taken steps to spruce up its own public restrooms in recent years. La Spata, who has been pushing for the toilets alongside Ald. Rossana Rodriguez Sanchez (33rd) for years, previously said it was something Chicago was "catching up" on. What are concerns over public restrooms? Some residents have voiced concerns that the public restrooms could attract crime or they would not be adequately cleaned. Those were similar issues JCDecaux faced and has begun to tackle in its other locations, the advertising giant said. According to the San Francisco Chronicle, after a single bathroom in San Francisco racked up more than 200 maintenance requests in less than four years of operation, the company began staffing and adapting the restrooms. That city's public works department said JCDecaux spends about $2.2 million per year maintaining a full fleet of public restrooms and staffing an attendant at each of them seven days a week from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. "to ensure the toilets are kept safe, clean and operational." It's unclear if Chicago's version will have an attendant. Related Chicago’s first self-cleaning public toilet coming to the Northwest Side next year, alderperson says

articles.title: Trump’s Illegal Campaign Ads Are an Admission of Defeat
articles.description: This week, one of the most talked-about stories has been President Donald Trump’s decision to spend taxpayer money on campaign ads that the administration is misleadingly characterizing as “public service announcements.” The move is vintage Trump in that the ads are both staggeringly corrupt—the administration is spending $20 million of the Department of Homeland Security’s money on them, in violation of the Hatch Act —and propagandizing slop. One ad, which uses a song without the artist’s permission, has Trump asking people, “ Love me .” Another warns of a “ final battle .” So far, the administration has only spent a fraction of the money that’s been allocated to this endeavor, so you can count on seeing many more iterations of these fake PSAs, which Trump is said to be guiding . But rather than think of this as some kind of flex, or one more scandalous abuse of the public trust, I want to suggest that what these ads represent is desperation—an acknowledgment that if Trump’s goose isn’t cooked yet, the pot is at least boiling. I also think, if anything, this fusillade of propaganda will likely backfire. These ads haven’t generated good news for Trump; very few people outside of the administration and its obvious sycophants have tried to defend them. Moreover, the media seems resistant to give this story the “both sides” treatment. As with Trump’s 25-minute prime-time ramble last July, the political press seems wise to what’s going on. Of that aforementioned speech, TNR editor Michael Tomasky said , the overall reaction to the president’s attempt to shine us on “tells us that that power he had over people and institutions a year or 15 months ago has evanesced.” I think these PSAs do little else than advertise that fact. I am not sure that Republican lawmakers necessarily agree with that assessment, but their own appraisals range from avoidant to withering. As MS NOW reported this week , “even congressional Republicans are expressing concern that the ads may violate the laws governing PSAs.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune is quoted in the piece as saying that he didn’t mind the message of the ad but believed “it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars.” That’s about the nicest thing any Republican who made their way into the story had to say about it, with Senator Mike Rounds saying, “It’s not something I would have done” and the outgoing Thom Tillis comparing it to Viktor Orbán. “I hate it,” said Tillis, bluntly. Trump’s midterm activities aren’t limited to these controversial ads. According to reports, the president is planning to spend 32 of the next 35 days on the road campaigning for Republicans. As Politico notes , many of his intended destinations suggest the GOP is in tremendous peril. Instead of swing states and traditionally competitive districts, Trump is visiting “bastions of conservatism” like Alabama, Oklahoma, Ohio, and Texas. He’s even going to trek out to Alaska, “a significant commitment of time and presidential resources that underscores how dire the situation is for Republicans.” As one GOP donor told Politico, “The problem is that the fires are everywhere right now.” The biggest question is whether Trump’s growing effort to further inject himself into the midterm cycle is going to help or hinder the electoral hopes of Republican lawmakers. In at least one contentious race, the Republican candidate is calling Trump an albatross. According to leaked audio obtained by The New York Times, Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton told a room full of donors that Trump’s weird midterm convention in early September—which was held in Texas, in the hopes it would boost Paxton—had the opposite effect. “So to be honest with you, the numbers—when we did that convention—it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.” (As Lawfare editor Eric Columbus pointed out , it’s also not good “when your 12-person private fundraiser includes someone who hates you enough to leak damaging audio.”) The Paxton audio is a potent snapshot of some larger trends. All across the country, we’re seeing stories of GOP strongholds edging toward collapse as onetime Trump voters bear the weight of his administration’s incompetence. There are daily reminders that other Republicans are trying to create distance between the president and their campaigns , and even defying him on key matters . On Wednesday, in fact, West Virginia Senator Jim Justice broke with Trump on the matter dearest to the president’s heart—his mass deportation machine. “Maybe we’re doing something wrong here or there,” he said. You think? Over the course of the year, as Trump’s approvals hit new lows and began to decimate the GOP’s midterm ambitions, I’ve tried to figure out what Trump and his fellow Republicans could do to reverse or even just arrest those trends. For a brief mad moment, I thought that the negotiated Memorandum of Understanding between the U.S. and Iran might provide a springboard Trump could use to extricate himself from his crazy war. This didn’t come to fruition. The truth is, to save their bacon, Republicans would have to do things they are genetically incapable of doing: improve people’s lives and fix the economy. As I pointed out two weeks ago , Republicans—despite their misgivings about Trump—are still touting their One Big Beautiful Bill Act: a document that says the wealthiest among us deserve thousands of extra dollars, and the rest of us deserve some measure of pain. It’s all adding up to defeat. The Cook Political Report says a Democratic takeover of the House is a “done deal” and that winning the Senate is “very realistic.” The Quinnipiac generic poll of the House has Democrats opening up a 51 percent to 39 percent lead , which are bloodbath numbers. The only headwind Democrats face is that while voters seem willing to give them their vote this year, they’re not as ready to give them their affection . Still, you’d rather be the Democrats right now than the GOP, who like Vice President JD Vance have been left begging voters for a “second chance” without understanding that they’ve already received that second chance—and they’ve blown it. This article first appeared in Power Mad , a weekly TNR newsletter authored by deputy editor Jason Linkins. Sign up here .

articles.title: Bangkok at breaking point as floods turn streets into stagnant lakes
articles.description: With 40 dead and a disaster declared across all 50 city districts, experts warn extreme flooding will only worsen across south-east Asia Bangkok is used to absorbing the sudden afternoon downpours that inundate the city during the rainy season. Even streets in many central high-rise districts can briefly turn into rivers, with rats and cockroaches racing out of sewers and taking temporary refuge on trees and buildings as the subterranean world is flushed out. But every city has a breaking point, and this year rain fell so fast and so hard that whole neighbourhoods of the Thai capital have been transformed, not into rivers, but stagnant lakes. In parts of the city, roughly 300mm of rain – the equivalent of half a year of average rainfall in London – fell in about two days. Continue reading...

articles.title: Don’t Worry, Everyone! Trump Says He Can Walk Up Ramps and Stairs
articles.description: The bar for America’s highest elected office keeps sinking. The nation’s totally healthy, very fit, 80-year-old president gave himself a little pat on the back Thursday after he managed to climb on the rally stage at the Peterbilt Motors manufacturing facility in Denton, Texas. The celebration came amid a dig at the health of his predecessor, former President Joe Biden. “Don’t forget, when Biden left the stage he spoke very shortly, like two minutes, one minute, as quickly as possible,” Trump said . “Could never find the stairs.” “I don’t have that problem. You know, these things—you know how many stairs they have?” Trump continued. “Look, I can go ramp, and I can go stair, I can go another stair, another stair in the back, I have a stair here—he could never find a stair.” "I can go ramp, I can go stairs" -- Trump's audience in Texas gives him an extremely tepid round of applause as he brags about being able to go up stairs without falling pic.twitter.com/SvQFajZZGO — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 1, 2026 Trump is the second oldest man to ever serve as America’s commander in chief. The octogenarian has spent hours at Walter Reed Medical Center on multiple occasions since he returned to office, has fallen asleep during more than a dozen critical meetings , appeared lost and disoriented around foreign heads of state, frequently slurs his speech, and seems to almost chronically suffer from discolored and bruised skin. His behavior has also grown increasingly erratic, as he has thrown cheap and petty insults at members of the press, challenged longstanding U.S. alliances, and even taken jabs at the pope. But Trump has nonetheless insisted that he is perfectly fit to keep the country’s most important job. Since 2024, the self-styled “stable genius” has “aced” several cognitive exams, though his recollections of the tests’ contents have called into question whether he actually took them at all. The American public is apparently wising up to Trump’s age: A national Strength in Numbers/Verasight poll conducted in July found that public perceptions of Trump’s mental health were on par with Biden’s, with 46 percent of respondents rating Trump’s mental sharpness as “poor.”
